course_description:
The course offers insights into worldwide constitutional systems, providing theoretical and practical bases for understanding, evaluating, and comparing different constitutions. It focuses on constitutional theory and practices, examining how principles manifest in supranational, federal, and devolutionary systems.

Students will be introduced to the theory, history, and practice of constitutional systems across the world. The course examines how different societies organise political power, protect constitutional values, and respond to common problems such as federalism, judicial review, constitutional amendment, and constituent power. Students will study both foundational questions of constitutionalism and concrete constitutional systems, including (but not limited to) the United States, Brazil, Switzerland, and Ethiopia. Through comparative analysis, the course explores how constitutional ideas travel across jurisdictions, how historical and cultural contexts shape constitutional design, and how similar constitutional structures may operate differently in practice.

This course will be taught in a 3-hour seminar format.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Course Aims

The course provides students with:

· An appropriate understanding of constitutional systems from around the world.

· Theoretical and practical bases for comprehending and evaluating different constitutional governments.

· Tools to examine specific constitutions enacted in different countries and contexts.

learning_outcomes.description: Identify an appropriate methodology of comparative law.
Understand the fundamental principles underlying constitutional and federal theories.
Distinguish constitutions according to the appropriate typologies.
Compare and evaluate different constitutions worldwide.

assessment_details.task_description: Students are required to complete an online test. The quiz consists of multiple-choice and/or true or false questions. The test will assess material covered in the seminars from weeks 2 to 8. This test is designed to assess the comprehension of the basic principles and concepts in comparative constitutional law, constitutional theory, and the US Constitution. This will ensure students understand the content covered to date and are satisfactorily following the learning materials. The test will open at 8 am Tuesday, 22 September , and close at 8 pm Wednesday, 23 September . The quiz will contain 20 questions. Each question is worth 1 mark. Incorrect answers are awarded no marks. The quiz will be time-limited to 30 minutes. Once started, the quiz must be completed in one sitting. Do not leave the test before clicking Save and Submit. There will be no opportunities for resits. Before sitting the test, please ensure that you have sufficient time and appropriate working conditions to complete it. assessment_details.title: Oral Presentation
assessment_details.due_date: The topics will vary each week, and allocations will be made in the first seminar (Week 1) of the course.
assessment_details.task_description: Students are required to deliver a short presentation on a specific feature or dimension of comparative constitutional law and constitutional theory. Topics will be set out on the Blackboard site with the dates on which they are to be presented. The topics will vary each week, and allocations will be made in the first seminar (Week 1) of the course. To present well, you should conduct comparative research and adopt a theoretical or analytical perspective on the history, development, or emerging issue related to the theme of your presentation and the country/constitution you have chosen. The presentation must be related to the constitution of a country other than Australia (except when indicated otherwise). You may discuss your topic choice with the course coordinator. There will be deductions (1 mark per 15 seconds) for exceeding the stipulated time limit. After each presentation, there is an opportunity for questions from fellow students and the lecturer. Responses to these questions will form part of the overall mark. This is to ensure authenticity and the level of knowledge and understanding of the topic. Presentations will typically be held in the final hour of the seminar. Each presentation must be accompanied by one e-poster (eg, one PowerPoint slide or PDF/JPEG image) and a list of references (bibliography). Students are required to submit their e-posters and bibliography through the course coordinator's email at least 12 hours before their presentation. The e-poster must be made with still images (that is, it must not contain any animations or motions). Text should be kept to a minimum in the poster. There should be no more than 50 words in the e-poster. References in the Bibliography should follow the AGLC4 style and rules. Students are marked according to their oral presentation, response to questions, bibliography/legal research, and e-poster. Students should be aware that, according to UQ policy, the presentations will be recorded. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Definitions & Methodology Introduction to the field of Comparative Constitutional Law: Is comparative law a proper field of law? What are the methodologies we can use to compare constitutions? What are some common terms and definitions we find in comparative constitutional law? Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Constitutionalism: Ancient and Modern Where does the idea of constitutionalism come from? Is constitutionalism an ancient or modern development? How has the idea of constitutionalism evolved? What are the main principles of constitutionalism? Learning outcomes: L02, L04
Constitutional Typologies How are different constitutions categorised? What are the distinct typologies and classifications of constitutions? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
Constitutional Formation & Constituent Power How are constitutions created? What is constituent power? Who has the legitimacy to enact a constitution? Learning outcomes: L02, L04

Constitutional Amendment & Judicial Review How are constitutions changed? Who can change a constitution? What processes are involved in materially or formally changing a constitution? What is the role of constitutional courts? How do constitutional courts operate? Learning outcomes: L02, L04
Federalism & Federations What is federalism? What is a federation? What are examples of federal countries? How are they similar, and how do they differ? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

The US Constitution: History and Key Features Why is the US Constitution so famous? How was it created? What are the key aspects of the US Constitution? What are some of its landmark constitutional cases? Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04
'Global North' Constitutions What are the key features of some of the 'Global North' Constitutions? Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04
'Global South' Constitutions What are the key features of some of the 'Global South' constitutions? Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04

The Australian Constitution in Context What can we learn about the Australian Constitution when looking abroad? What principles and provisions have we inherited from abroad? What is distinctive about our Constitution? Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04
